may there be prosperity!
[The arising of detachment]
In the *Uttaravātula*, in the dialogue between Śiva and the Pramatha [attendants],
all the Gaṇas assembled upon Mount Mandara before the Supreme Lord.
The future divine play of the stainless, all-pervading Lord, which destroys worldly existence.
Those desirous of knowledge respectfully prayed to the Supreme Śiva.
Thus entreated by the hosts, Śiva spoke playfully.
The stainless mobile liṅga is situated in the center of the wheel at the tip of the nose.
Blazing, it appeared in person, bestowing the sovereignty of liberation. || 3 ||
But this mobile liṅga of mine is a hundred times superior to me.
O Gaṇas, I am endowed with supreme power, yet this [world] is beyond power.
But this is to be known as partless (niṣkala), whereas I am with parts (sakala), O lords of the Gaṇas.
"I am endowed with color, O hosts, yet this [reality] transcends color. (5)
In the beginning, that mobile liṅga is remembered as being "stainless" (nirañjana).
In the Tretā age, this deity was fashioned and is thus celebrated as "Nirmāya."
And in the Dvāpara age, it is indeed renowned as the Niṣkala (the Partless).
In the Kali age, he is known as Prabhū; indeed, these are his names in sequence.
In the Kali age, the seat (pīṭha) of that Lord Deva is in Kalyāṇapattana.
It was fashioned by the multitude of Pramathas, headed by Basaveśa. || 8 ||
The Trika is the triple consciousness, the void, consisting of the nature of Nāda, Bindu, and Kalā.
That Praṇava is indeed devoid of qualities; it is entirely void and exists in three ways.
It is considered such because it contains the threefold inclinations and because it is that very seat (pīṭha).
And it is celebrated everywhere on earth as the "Empty Lion Throne. || 10 ||
Having gone to the glorious temple of Basava out of devotion to his devotees, he—
Then the Lord, the Master, the King of the Pramathas, ascended the throne.
Through his grace, he bestowed the initiation of knowledge upon Basaveśvara and the other leaders.
Having composed this work in the form of a compendium of the essence of all Vedāntas.
Having clearly awakened the state of the perfect identity between the Liṅga and the body;
Then, having bestowed upon them grace and all else that removes every impurity, [he departed].
Having caused all those present there to drink [the sacred water] marked with the name of the illustrious Cannabasava.
[He saw] a celibate student (brahmacārin), most venerable due to his possession of the sixfold excellence of the stages of life.
Having looked upon him with compassion and having summoned him to his presence, the Lord—
One's own seal, one's own hermitage, the sacred seat (pīṭha), and the book of conduct. || 15 ||
The preservation of this doctrine is indeed maintained through the tradition in this very way.
"Act for the sake of uplifting the world; increase the lineage of your disciples.
Having thus instructed him, the Lord, the stainless Sovereign, then [departed].
Wandering upon the earth together with the leaders of the Gaṇas for the sake of the welfare of the world. || 17 ||
Likewise, for the sake of destroying the multitude of sins of his devotees, [he bestows] initiation, instruction, and so forth.
Then, having made arrangements in all regions according to his will, he concealed [himself].
Having spread my Dharma, he will come back to me once again.
Then those born of that lineage on earth were endowed with the practice of that [conduct]. || 19 ||
Having wandered over the entire surface of the earth for the sake of bestowing grace upon all devotees.
Having established monasteries in various places, he also performed initiations and other rites.
Having divided the saṃskāras into many parts, they will uphold my doctrine.

[The characteristic of the Nirābhāra:
In the *Sūkṣmāgama*, chapter 12,
it is stated that for those who practice the Nirābhāra, there are six qualities considered to be ornaments.
Or, if it is short by one [syllable], it is called *dārī*. || 1 ||
Detachment, the perfection of knowledge, celibacy, austerity resplendent with heat, compassion, and right conduct—these six are proclaimed. (2)
If a spy who bears the outward mark should abandon the six qualities of refined conduct, he is not a man of good conduct; he is merely a spy, and in truth, a night-walker (a demon).
Born as a Liṅgin Brāhmaṇa, wearing the Liṅga and endowed with ritual action,
one should become free from desire for women and proceed to the state beyond all appearances.
How can one who follows the path of the hero and always maintains his conduct, yet does not practice it and eats food [obtained by begging], be a possessor of Vīraśaiva? || 5 ||
O Goddess of gods, if all devotees are always honored for their skill in right conduct and their livelihoods, then why indeed would moving beings not be born [in such a state]? 6.
Those devoted to the knowledge of the Carādas have become intent on bestowing curses;
they do not become true devotees nor experts in the paths of the Vīras.
A hero who possesses right conduct is a true Vīraśaiva;
however, one who lacks right conduct, even if he be a lord of the Gaṇas, is to be censured by the lords of the Gaṇas.
Through devotion to improper conduct, the occurrence of a great sin (mahāpātaka) arises;
O Goddess, due to the emergence of such a great sin, one becomes a partaker of torments.
Whether through ignorance, anger, or even delusion, a human being who commits many sins becomes a vessel for torment. (10)
O Īśānī, for the devotees who are Vīraśaivas and are ever free from worldly burdens,
the saffron-colored garment is the ornament of their own cherished Liṅga.
The thread for the linga is white, the garment of Śambhu is white,
and the fine cloth is white for those who are intent upon the meditation on Me.
O Maheśvarī, one who is free from objective support and detached is worthy of worship by the world;
yet, without saffron-colored garments, he should not wear white clothing.
Animals are superior in intelligence to worms, insects, and moths; humans are even more excellent than animals, and among them, the twice-born are the most excellent. (14)

Among the twice-born, the Brahmins are superior; among Brahmins, those whose intellect is fixed on sacrifice; among those whose intellect is fixed on sacrifice, the performers [of the rites]; and superior to them are the renunciants (saṃnyāsins). 15.
Among them, the wise are superior; among them, the worshippers of Śaṅkara are superior;
and among them, O fortunate one, those who are united with my Liṅga-body are the most excellent. (16)

A man who possesses knowledge of the six stages (ṣaṭsthala) is superior to those whose limbs are attached to the Liṅga; indeed, there is no one superior even to him at any time throughout the three worlds. 17.
He is always to be saluted and worshipped by those who desire to conquer the cycle of worldly existence;
what is the use of saying more, my child? He is indeed this very person, without a doubt. (18)
O Daughter of Śaṅkara, previously Suyaśas’ beloved spoke these words in the singular number with joy to the prince; today, however, he has been enlightened here.
Whatever place a Vīraśaiva graces for even a moment, contemplate with certainty that this place is indeed the abode of the Liṅga. || 20 ||
Born from the womb of Vīraśaiva is the supportless (nirābhārī) Maheśvara;
O Goddess, the father of the supportless one is the Vīraśaiva Gaṇeśvara. || 21 ||
The Vīraśaiva is indeed the form of the father, the very form of the mother, the form of the guru, and the stainless (nirañjana) form of the Liṅga. || 22 ||
The supreme teacher Nirābhārī was a reciter of the Nigamas and Āgamas;
he emerged from the Western Seat through the power of the cause of devotion.
The world-purifying Jāhnavī, who flows from his lotus feet, became this Gaṅgā, a garland of skulls, for the Vīraśaiva. (24)
O Goddess, devoid of ritual action and likewise devoid of external marks, I am also devoid of form, existing solely as the nature of pure knowledge.
O Goddess, my devotee who possesses the Vīraśaiva tradition, having always become one who bears a body, who bears the *liṅga*, and whose nature consists of action and knowledge, wanders about.
I am superior to all, and these Vīraśaivas are my lords.
O Goddess, for them there is nothing superior; this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt. || 27 ||
O my beloved, if that person in whom a lack of proper conduct exists, being devoid of the sacred thread, is declared by my word to be the lowest of men; 28.
The profundity of all phenomena proceeds from pure progression;
by the absence of progression, O fair-faced one, it destroys all phenomena. (29)
In the Śaṅkarasaṃhitā, Chapter 83:
One should wear the patched garment known as patience, the ash-smeared body, the water-pot of compassion, and the beautiful staff of truth and knowledge. (51)
One should beg for the alms-vessel of dispassion and the alms of devotion from pure men who are devoted to the union of the Linga and the body (the Guru) and who are endowed with virtuous conduct.
As he wanders in this manner, these become his possessions:
learning is his wife, contentment is his son, and indeed, forgiveness is his female servant. (53)
Devotion is considered the mother, right conduct the father, truth the grandson, tranquility the friend, detachment the well-wisher, self-restraint the teacher, and faith the sister. (54)
The injury of servitude is said to be the slave; non-stealing is proclaimed [as another]. Benevolence and the like are declared to be his sons, and this Dharma is considered his vehicle. (55)
Knowledge is the body, and likewise the field; reflection has all things as its domain.
Liberation is the place that is easily accessible for one who is united with the limbs of the vital-organ liṅga.
O child, having taken up these possessions with a pure mind, a man, filled with consciousness and bliss, may wander this earth. (57)

(81) In the chapter [on the Atimārga]: One who has transcended the stages of life (atyāśramī), being connected with the Prāṇaliṅga, should carry a girdle of ashes, a patched garment, a water-pot, an alms-bowl, and a staff. || 48 ||
Whosoever indeed possesses these five great mudrās, having approached them for refuge, one should worship each with one's entire being. (49)
O child, that Dharma in which the five mudrās are present is always to be saluted and worshipped by those who possess the prāṇaliṅga.
In the seventh chapter of the *Sūkṣmāgama*: "I shall explain the doctrine of the Nirābhāsa; listen with a concentrated mind. (75)
For a living being, action is said to be twofold: merit and demerit.
Because he has laid down the burden of action, he is remembered as "Nirābhāra" (the Burdenless One).
Whether wearing matted locks, a shaven head, or a topknot, and clad in saffron robes,
he should be free from desire, identified with his own true nature, subsisting on alms, and devoid of fear.
Silent, endowed with compassion for all beings, and free from worldly burdens—he is thus praised.
Indeed, whatever greatness belongs to those with matted hair, that very same greatness belongs to those with shaven heads. (78)
Wearing a patched garment and a water-pot, endowed with sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads,
and carrying a staff and a loincloth, he is known as the Nirābhāra.
One should worship the Liṅga with wild leaves, flowers, and fruits, free from desire, anger, and other passions, having conquered the mountains of pride through the knowledge of Śiva. (80)
A wandering mendicant should go for alms only as much as is needed to fill his own belly;
he should practice the "bee-like" method of begging, remaining mobile and devoted to compassion.
O Goddess, one should not eat food from only one person, for that causes fault;
O Pārvatī, just as a honeybee takes nectar from flowers.
Likewise, one should beg from a householder according to the rules for fasting;
or one may eat food obtained from a single source, provided it is requested with respect by the virtuous.
These devotees of Maheśvara are to be honored by householders;
any worship performed without them becomes fruitless.
A wandering ascetic (jaṅgama) should not accumulate material possessions anywhere at all.
Filled with compassion, he should give what has been offered to his devotees and to the poor. || 85 ||
If one who has transcended the stages of life (atyāśramī) should live by increasing his wealth through gifts of gold, jewels, and other such things, he is the foremost among sinners. (86)
Whether wearing matted locks, a topknot, or being shaven-headed, he who, though endowed with the five seals (mudrās), engages in sexual union with women is my enemy; of this there is no doubt. (87)
One who has transcended the castes and stages of life (ativarṇāśramī), being shaven-headed and possessing the yoga of the vital-force-liṅga on his body,
should not wear a head-cloth nor should he wear a turban.

Just as a linga that is cracked, broken, or otherwise defective is not worshipped, so too a *jaṅgama* who has fallen away from the conduct, vows, and observances pertaining to the linga is not to be worshipped. (89)
This should be mutually honored with a mind imbued with the nature of Śiva;
for he who, seeing one mobile being, does not offer salutation to another mobile being, [is at fault]. (90)
He who harms a living being is undoubtedly one who harms me;
O Daughter of Śaṅkara, he who out of delusion hates a living being hates me.
Therefore, even among one another in the realm of the moving and the stationary, they should be honored.
Devotion to Śiva, knowledge of Śiva, the mudrā of Śiva, and the vow of Śiva—[these are the marks]. 92.
Faith in the worship of the Śiva-liṅga and the cessation of other activities—
wherever these virtues exist, that person is free from both burden and lack of burden.

He who is perfected in the knowledge of the six locations, who possesses the meditative absorption of the six limbs and their sub-limbs, and who perceives others as his own self—he is indeed I, without a doubt. (94)
O Pārvatī, wherever one who is devoted to Vīraśaiva resides, that place is a sacred site (tīrtha), that is true penance, and that is peace; there I always abide.
O Pārvatī, for these [devotees], there is no need for pilgrimages to sacred sites and the like elsewhere;
one who possesses the union of the Liṅga and the body should abandon all longing for states such as Kailāsa.
One should avoid that place where there is worship of other deities, and one should never take refuge in a person who is devoid of devotion to Śiva. 97.
Among the recipient, the giver, and the gift, that which is marked with the auspicious sign of Śiva is most beautiful;
what is marked with the sign of Śiva should be accepted, while anything else is equal to the food of a Cāṇḍāla or a rogue.

For devotees who are united with the body of the Liṅga, there is no need for lunar days, nor constellations, nor astrological conjunctions and so forth, nor even the science of physiognomy (sāmudrika). || 99 ||
One should perceive everything as consisting of Śiva; no other state of being exists.
Knowledge of the reality of the relationship between the Liṅga and the Aṅga is the means to liberation. 100.
For those of us who are united with the body of the Liṅga, that alone shall be liberation;
therefore, everyone should always perform the worship of the Liṅga with devotion.
In the *Pārameśvarāgama*, chapter eight, the Lord said:
"Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain that which you ask of me."
The greatness of my doctrine, together with its secret essence and in full detail.
O Goddess of gods, that which is called heroism is like a warrior-hero in battle;
likewise, in this doctrine, one is a hero through true devotion and firm detachment.
Freed from the three types of craving, devoted to knowledge and higher realization, and endowed with firm dispassion—those heroes are the Śiva-yogins. (3)
O Goddess, those who are blind to the sight of the forms of other men’s wives are the true wearers of the *liṅga*;
even the young and the learned are heroes, the yogins of Śiva.
O Goddess, those who are mute regarding the censure of others' faults, even if they are all-knowing, are eloquent; they are the heroes, the yogins of Śiva. || 5 ||
Those who are eunuchs toward the beloved wives of others, who are lame in causing pain to others,
and who are tongueless in tasting flavors— those heroes are the yogins of Śiva.
Free from pride, devoid of hypocrisy, endowed with non-violence, patience, and straightforwardness, and devoted to the service of the teacher— those heroes are the yogins of Śiva.
Those heroes who possess freedom from egoism through purity, self-restraint, and steadfastness, and who maintain an even mind toward all things— they are the yogis of Śiva.

Those heroes who are devoted to speaking the truth and observing their vows, who are intent on non-stealing as their wealth, and whose nature is characterized by non-possessiveness—they are the yogis of Śiva. 13.

Those who do not feel enmity toward those superior to themselves, who are free from malice toward their equals, and who do not treat those inferior to them with contempt—those heroes are the yogins of Śiva. 14.
Free from rivalry, envy, and contempt, with tranquil minds and constantly devoted to meditation upon me—those heroes are the yogis of Śiva. 15.
When one awakens from sleep while still mindful of the Guru Śiva,
having risen, O Goddess, one should contemplate me, the Guru, in the form of the Liṅga.

O Goddess of gods, having prepared whatever is available— such as leaves, flowers, unbroken grains (akṣata), and so forth— the practitioner should perform the worship on the previous day at the first hour of dawn.
One should worship Śivā constantly at dawn, at midday, and likewise in the evening;
however, if one is unable [to worship at all three times], one should worship both in the evening and in the morning.

If one is able, one should worship at dawn; otherwise, O Śivā, one should worship during the twilight (saṃdhyā). One should worship constantly in whatever manner accords with one's inclination. || 21 ||
Worship is constant throughout the three periods of time, while worship at midday is optional.
O Śivā, worship is performed daily in the morning and evening, and also occasionally at other times.
If one is incapable and without assistance, one may always worship according to one's desire.
He who, though capable, does not perform [this duty], shall dwell in the Raurava hell. || 23 ||
And even though the collection of conditions is present and my worship possesses efficacy, [the result does not arise].
He who, being lustful and afflicted by sensual objects, does not worship out of deceit, [is lost]. || 24 ||
Falling away from both action and knowledge, he is submerged in the ocean of suffering.
He shall dwell in the terrible Raurava hell as long as the moon and stars exist. || 25 ||
Uṣas refers to the period of time extending up to one muhūrta prior to the rising of the sun.
That time should be known as the hour of worship, which brings about the attainment of the state of Śiva. || 26 ||
Alternatively, immediately after the rising of the sun, one should worship Śiva.
Likewise at midday and in the evening, having performed the observation of the stars.
O beloved, having performed the morning worship, including the recitation of mantras and hymns of praise, [one should proceed].
Having first prostrated before his guru, he should go out to wander for alms.
One should wander among those very devotees who bear the sectarian marks (liṅgin) and are Śiva-yogins.
As much as he desires, whether it be cooked or even uncooked, at the door of his house.
Or one with a bell tied to his foot, or a bell-bearer, or a bearer of the victory-bell.
And Śaṅkha, or Śṛṅgināda, or even Daṇḍaghaṇṭa, while wandering about—
Adorned with necklaces of rudrākṣa beads and clad in a patched garment and a woolen blanket.
Having informed the householders by means of some sign or sound. || 32 ||
Remembering the duty toward the guru, the bearer of the emblem (liṅgin) should command, "Beg for alms."
Whether it be a householder or a housewife, having bowed down, one should bring the mobile [image]. || 33 ||
Having worshipped him with the thought that he is Śiva, one should dismiss him once he is fully satisfied.
If it is brought uncooked, one should cook it and then offer it to me. || 34 ||
If it should be cooked and brought, let it be offered to me and I shall eat it.
There is no restriction to eating only once a day, nor fasting and the like, nor any vow. // 35 //
Just as one traveling on the roads [endures] cold, wind, heat, and so forth; || 38 ||
Having endured this lightly, O Goddess of gods, he attains his own state.
Neither among women, nor among those unworthy, nor even in births characterized by unrighteousness. || 38 ||
One who follows Vīraśaivism is not born among the lowly, such as animals and the like. || 39 ||
In the ninth chapter,
one who enjoys the happiness obtained by destiny and is devoted to the worship of Śiva.
Having attained the state of Vīraśaiva, one easily reaches final liberation.
A single bowl for alms, a single patched garment, and a black woolen blanket.
The staff, the sacred sound, and devotion to Śiva are the characteristics of a Vīraśaiva. || 46 ||
Peace is the culmination, the subduing of beings, and the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind.
The identity with the Lord in all things is the defining characteristic of a Vīraśaiva. || 45 ||
Neither sense objects, nor enjoyments, nor kinsmen can protect one at all.
When Śaṅkara exists, there is no such thing as poverty for one who has attained perfection; this is the final certainty.
In the forest there are leaves, and in the river there are sweet waters.
There are hands and feet, and my own body is free from affliction.
For him there is no exertion, nor service, nor toil, nor loss of wealth.
Having propitiated me, the Lord, with ease, the wise man attains the auspicious state.
Having attained the Vīramata, he who would abandon it otherwise should be cut down by me.
Having seized the tail of a dog, he desires to cross the ocean.
Having learned the scriptures from the mouth of the guru, he took up the saffron-colored robes and staff.
Having abandoned the household life, one should go forth as a renunciant—whether wearing a topknot, being shaven-headed, or having matted hair.
In the fifteenth chapter:
One should always dwell in the forest, avoiding association with villages and devotees.
He should not enter a city, a village, or the house of householders.
O Maheśvarī, if a devotee, having brought alms, should offer them [to you].
One should not think of taste nor of pleasure, nor of what is beneficial or harmful.
One should not look upon the face of women, nor should one listen to their words regarding the Dharma.
O Goddess, I do not desire social gatherings with other people, nor wandering about according to my own whims.
One should sleep on the ground and avoid a bed for the sake of auspicious rest; one should wear discolored clothing if one desires whatever [is sought]. 59.
He may be shaven-headed, or wear matted locks, or a topknot, or even have disheveled hair.
Whether he be shaven-headed or wear a topknot, if he should apply oil to his body according to his own desire; 60.
If one who wears matted hair should never, at any time, perform an oil massage.
If he previously wore matted hair, he should not undergo a haircut again. || 61 ||
If a Śaiva ascetic (liṅgin) who wears the topknot (śikhin) should perform an oil massage at his own will, [he incurs a fault].
One should not touch oil that has come into contact with a leather vessel, for it possesses the nature of intoxicants.
One should not look at spectacles such as dancing and the like; one should dwell in solitude.
Proceeding correctly according to the scripture and the words of the teacher.
O Śivā, while I dwell in the world, he is my disciple and he is my teacher.
In the Suprabodhāgama.
O Pārvatī, listen to the characteristics of the hero who is free from appearances.
All snakes, sandalwood, and so forth, as well as women and the like, are great bliss. || 1 ||
Having set aside one's own mind, one should always place that [consciousness] in the Supreme Śiva.
But having realized the one [Self] within his own self, he is freed from all attachments. || 2 ||
The staff, the loincloth, the saffron robe, the matted hair, the yoga-accoutrements, and the water-pot.
Or else, having shaved his head, he remains without clothing.
Equipped with a seat of antelope skin and clothed in saffron robes, he should wander.
Holding a gourd-shell bowl, he shall become a naked devotee of Śiva.
He was devoted to tasting the grace of Śiva obtained by chance.
Having renounced land, wealth, and daughters through body, speech, and mind. || 5 ||
Having abandoned the home, monasteries, and the dwellings of men and others.
He should go into exile in forests, mountain caves, and similar places.
He who treats the life of the world as a blade of grass and has abandoned worldly conduct.
And likewise, one who has abandoned the excellent lineage, as well as the colors and so forth described in the Sūtras.
By the play of the Self-born One, I am he who has realized the Self, knowing "I am Brahman."
Becoming free from the sense of "mine" and devoid of physical form, he was entirely separated from contact with his wife.
He is without cause, without blemish, free from conceptual construction, and devoid of activity.
Free from conceptual proliferation, free from indolence, and devoid of passion, hatred, and the like.
And regarding that which is prohibited and that which is of the nature of a prescription, he should remain single-minded.
In the dwellings of householders devoted to ritual action, there is both auspicious and inauspicious.
In matters such as marriages and the like, as well as in the placement of corpses and so forth.
And having arrived, he should dwell for one day in a city or village. || 11 ||
He should subsist by begging for food and drink at three houses.
If it has been given, one may enjoy it; otherwise, one should not cause distress.
He may ride in a palanquin, provided he avoids riding on horseback.
And having become a pedestrian, he should always wander throughout the circle of the earth.
Free from both instruction and curse toward those who are non-devotees as well as devotees.
He should eat but once a day and should always remain possessed of dispassion. || 14 ||
True knowledge is considered to be a daughter, contentment a son, and dispassion a kinsman. || 15 ||
Forbearance alone is his retinue, and peace is said to be his friend.
Devotion is my mother, virtuous conduct is my father, and truth is my son. || 16 ||
Faith alone is declared to be the daughter-in-law, and likewise, non-destruction is the slave.
Dharma is said to be the vehicle, as are right conduct and self-restraint. || 17 ||
Non-violence is declared to be the maidservant here, and the excellent virtues such as friendliness are her grandsons.
Knowledge alone shall be the body, and inquiry alone the field. || 18 ||
With a mind always resolved that liberation alone is the supreme goal, he remains steadfast.
A patched garment, a water-pot, a staff, and indeed a bowl for alms. || 19 ||
One should carry these five—the ash-pot and the external mudrās.
Having held it immediately thereafter according to its respective mantra, || 20 ||
One should indeed wear the other five mudrās on the inner side.
Equanimity itself shall be the patched garment, and likewise, knowledge shall be the staff.
His water-pot was indeed detachment itself, and his alms-bowl was dispassion.
One should likewise wear a pellet of ashes on the forehead even at the end [of one's life], maintaining only forbearance.
Having indeed adopted such Śaiva garbs, one should always conduct oneself accordingly.
The worship of Śiva, the wearing of the triple marks (tripuṇḍra), and the smearing with sacred ash.
He should perform the recitation of Śiva-mantras and remain devoted to the meditation upon Śiva.
He is always endowed with the union of the Liṅga and the Aṅga, as well as with ritual action, knowledge, and so forth.
But likewise, without having practiced elixirs and the like, as well as buying and selling;
One should consult the physician, the astrologer, and matters concerning worldly legal affairs. (25)
Having abandoned sense objects and the like, one should thereafter become dispassionate.
One should abandon the ground in the middle of the forest called existence, which is parched by greed. || 26 ||
The Śuddhavīra-Śivācāryas on earth are endowed with the five mudrās.
They may move about according to their own will and are to be saluted by devotees from all sides.
Instruction should be given to men who come [to one] by the power of destiny. || 6 ||
Instruction in knowledge should be given, and not instruction in ritual action.
The Nirābhāras and Vīraśaivas are all worthy of worship; of this there is no doubt. || 7 ||
They never possess the power to inflict punishment upon them at any time. || 8 ||
In the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*:
He says that one should not abandon the practice of those dharmas, even if one is dispassionate.
For Dharma alone is the cause of the complete accomplishment of all things.
Even though he is free from desire, the great yogi should not abandon the path of Dharma. || 1 ||
To the objection, "What need have the knowers of reality for the practice of dharma?", he says:
Even though a yogi is satiated with the nectar of knowledge, he should not abandon dharma.
For worldly people indeed follow the conduct they observe in the great ones. || 2 ||
In the *Sūkṣmāgama*, chapter 12:

Seeing him arrived at the house, one should rise and salute him.
One should respectfully dispel his fatigue with fans and other such means. || 46 ||
Having prostrated, one should say "Welcome" and perform the washing of the feet.
First, one should worship with perfumes and flowers, and thereafter wash [the image].
One should meditate on Rudra upon the thumb and recollect Śaṅkara upon the index finger.
In the middle [finger], [he should place] Mahādeva; in the ring finger, Tryambaka. || 48 ||
One should place Īśāna on the little finger, and Kapardin upon the feet.
Beneath the feet is the five-faced one; at the two ankles are Ugra and Bharga.
Having meditated upon everything as consisting of the Liṅga, one should touch the foot of a mobile bearer of the Liṅga.
One should drink water that has been rinsed, and having drunk it, one should hold it upon the head.
One should not let a drop fall downward with the water used for washing the feet.
Furthermore, one should worship him again in due order with perfumes, flowers, incense, and other offerings. || 51 ||
Whether it be a woman or even a man, in all cases, one should honor a guest.
Men should place perfumes and other offerings in the hand of men, and women in the hand of women.
In that regard, there is no distinction of caste among those who possess the signs [of realization], the Śiva-yogins.
Nor is there any fault in seeing or touching; everything is indeed auspicious in the Auspicious One.
The Guru is the mobile liṅga, and his feet are the source of grace and the holy water.
In my body are the Vibhūti, the Rudrākṣa, and the five-syllabled mantra.
These men, heroic devotees of Maheśvara, are endowed with the eightfold enclosure.
O Goddess, assuming my form, they wander upon the surface of the earth. || 55 ||
One whose mind is struck by the notion that it is "leftover" food does not eat what has been consumed by a bearer of sectarian marks.
One should not wash that vessel, nor should one cause it to be broken.
If anyone eats from a vessel that has been used by a bearer of sectarian marks (liṅgin), it is considered leftover food.
In the absence of a vessel, at the same time, and so forth, all those wearing sectarian marks (liṅgins) eat together.
In the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*, the section on the majesty of the Guru follows; here is the introduction: Now, by one established in grace, the section on the majesty of the Guru is to be understood.
The verse explains: "In this regard, the Guru alone is the cause of all rites for attaining accomplishment."
For Mahādeva, in the form of the Guru, is present there in person. || 1 ||
Regarding the explanation here: in this world, the Guru alone is the cause of all accomplishments (*siddhi*) characterized by worldly enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*mokṣa*).
This is because of the statement in the *Śivarahasya*: "There is nothing superior to the disciple, and nothing superior to the Guru.
Therefore, the meaning is that the Supreme Lord himself is present, having manifested directly in the form of the Guru. || 1 ||
Introduction: Now, one might ask, "Since Śiva is partless (*niṣkala*), for what purpose does he manifest in the form of the teacher with parts (*sakalaguru*)?
To this, the verse says: "For Mahādeva is partless, a great ocean of eternal knowledge."
In the form of the Guru, he becomes the benefactor of all. || 2 ||
The explanation is as follows: although the Supreme Lord is the ocean of eternal knowledge, being partless and without limbs,
he becomes the benefactor of all by assuming the form of a Guru, appearing as one who possesses limbs such as hands and feet.
The meaning is that he shines for the sake of favoring the worlds. || 2 ||
Introduction: Therefore, he states that there is no difference between the Guru and Śiva:
The verse: He who is Śiva is to be known as the Guru; he who is the Guru is remembered as Śiva.
One who has attained knowledge and possesses great intelligence should not make any distinction between these two.

The meaning is that one should not, with a subtle vision, create any distinction (*antara*) or difference (*bheda*) between those two—the teacher and the teaching—because the teacher is non-different from Śiva by virtue of being the bestower of the knowledge that causes liberation; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that knowledge would not arise. || 3 ||

Introduction: As it is stated in the scripture, "Just as I am the teacher of all worlds together with Ambikā," one should worship the venerable Guru who is equal to Śiva, rather than describing him as being like ordinary people; thus he says in the verse: "One should not say he is equal to others on account of the similarity of hands, feet, and so forth."
The teacher, pure and abiding as the very form of Śiva, is the bestower of knowledge. || 4 ||

One should not speak of the venerable Guru— who is pure exposition, whose inner being is stainless, who illuminates the knowledge of Śiva, and who exists in the form of Umā and Maheśvara— as being equal to ordinary people by virtue of the similarity of his hands, feet, and other limbs. || 4 ||
Introduction: To the question "What happens because of that?", he says in a verse: "By the disparagement of the teacher, the attainment of the highest good is obstructed."
Therefore, for the attainment of the supreme good, one should worship him with a concentrated mind.

The attainment of the highest good, characterized by worldly enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*mokṣa*), is obstructed by disparaging the teacher’s exposition and by speaking like an ordinary person; therefore, for the sake of attaining that supreme good and for the attainment of enjoyment and liberation, one should, being composed and single-minded, [serve] that venerable Guru.
The meaning is that one should worship. || 5 ||

Introduction: Now, elucidating the meaning of the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad verse, "He who has supreme devotion for the Lord, and as for the Lord, so for the Guru," he concludes the section on the greatness of the Guru with this verse: "For one devoid of devotion to the Guru, devotion to Śiva does not arise."
Therefore, just as there is devotion to Śiva, so too should there be devotion to the Guru.
The explanation is clear. || 6 ||
Thus ends the section on the greatness of the Guru;
now follows the section on the greatness of the *jaṅgama* (the living embodiment).
As an introduction: now he elucidates the section on the *jaṅgama* as an object of direct experience, by virtue of the greatness of the Guru-liṅga.
Verse: [This is] the excellence of the majesty of the *liṅga* mounted by both teacher and disciple.
Everything arises from consciousness whose nature is intelligence; therefore, it is said that mobile beings possess superiority. || 1 ||

According to the Śruti, "The teacher is the prior form, the disciple is the subsequent form, and the transmission of knowledge is the junction"; thus, through the realization that the entire phenomenal universe is the glory of the Śiva-liṅga situated between the teacher and the disciple, and through the realization that it consists of the activity of consciousness (*cit-kriyā*) arising from its nature as consciousness (*cid-rūpa*).

The superiority of the *jaṅgama* (the living teacher) is now described. Through the cultivation of identity (*tādātmya-bhāvanā*) with the desired objects of life regarding both the Guru and the disciple, and by attaining the greatness of the installed *liṅga*, the realization that the entire universe consists of Śiva and Śakti is itself the meaning of the superiority of the *jaṅgama*. || 1 ||

Introduction: Now, regarding the question "Among which [beings] are those mobile?", he says the following verse: "But those who, through their excellence, know Śiva as the illuminator of the universe..."
But they are proclaimed as "mobile" (jaṅgama) by virtue of their own essential nature. || 2 ||

The commentary on that [is as follows]: according to the Śruti, "By His light all this shines," those who [worship] Śiva— the illuminator of the universe who, through His own powers of consciousness (*cit*) and action (*kriyā*), manifests the phenomenal world (*prapañca*)—
[regard Him] as pre-eminently the meaning of both the words "all" and "not-all," which are the effects of Māyā.
Because it is eternal by virtue of being ever-present,
and because this life-force's qualities of sentience and agency are eternal; otherwise,
being devoid of knowledge regarding its own object, it would result in insentience, like the radiance of a crystal or similar objects.

The meaning is that those who, through the firm conviction that [the Lord] is not distinct from themselves— because He is their own essential nature (nijasvabhāva), which is the reality of the Self (ātmatattva) common to both the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara)— know Him as their own true self (svarūpa), they are the "mobile" (jaṅgama). || 2 ||
Introduction: Now, he establishes the greatness of the *jaṅgama* (living deity), who is renowned as a Śiva-yogi, by means of five sūtras.
Verse: Those who, through the yoga of Śiva, perceive the web of the world as being of the nature of consciousness (*cid-rūpa*).
Those whose contact with impurity has been shaken off are remembered as Śiva-yogins.
Regarding the explanation: those who are mobile deities [attain] the universe through union with Śiva (*śivayoga*).

Since, in the absence of a connection with Śiva, the universe would result in being a mere mental construction due to its externality to consciousness, a connection with Śiva must indeed be admitted. Furthermore, that [connection] is not of the nature of a conjunction (*saṃyoga*), because...

Since it has been established that [the relationship] is possible only between two things situated in different locations by virtue of action being prior [to the result], and because there is no external space apart from Brahman, [the relationship] is of the nature of identity (*tādātmya*). Those who see—that is, those who know—that the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*) is the very essence of the activity of consciousness (*citkriyā*), have shaken off the touch of impurity; they are free from the connection with the impurities such as *āṇavamala*.
The meaning is that they are known as "Śiva-yogins. || 3 ||
(Verse: The cause for the total destruction of the darkness of the terrible cycle of existence.
Those who possess the knowledge of Śiva are considered Śiva-yogins.
The meaning is that those who possess the commentary—which wards off the terrifying darkness of saṃsāra—and the knowledge of the supreme Śiva, are considered and remembered as Śiva-yogins. || 4 ||
Introduction: Now, as to what they are like and how they abide, he says in a verse: "Having conquered desire, having conquered anger, and having severed the knot of delusion."
To the virtuous Śiva-yogins, a clod of earth, a stone, and gold are all the same.
They are equal toward both enemy and friend, having directly realized that their own self is Śiva.
Free from longing and devoid of ego, the Śiva-yogins abide [in this state].
The explanation is clear. || 5 || 6 ||
The introductory commentary: He states that those endowed with the knowledge characterized as described above are indeed Śiva himself—verse:
"For the knowledge of Śiva is difficult to attain, and the contemplation of Śiva is difficult to attain."
And those who possess this pair are directly of the nature of Śiva.

The exposition of Śiva-knowledge, the knowledge of Śiva’s supremacy, the contemplation of Śiva, and the realization—through the aforementioned reasonings—that one is oneself Śiva: these two are difficult to attain. The meaning is that those who possess this pair are the very embodiment of Śiva. || 7 ||
Introduction: Now, moreover, he describes their greatness in two verses. Verse:
Wherever the dust from the tips of the feet of the Śiva-yogins falls...
That very dwelling is meritorious and purifying for householders.
The sight of Śiva-yogins brings about all accomplishments for men.
Touching it pacifies sin; worshipping it is the means to liberation. || 9 ||

The explanation is as follows: "of the Śiva-yogins" means of the *jaṅgama-devas*; "of householders" means of those living as *gṛhasthas*; "meritorious" means a field of merit; "purifying" means sacred.
The remainder is clear. || 8 || 9 ||
Introduction: Now, it is said that through association with such Śiva-yogins, there is the accomplishment of all desired aims.
The verse: [This occurs] through the great ones who know the intent of Śiva and who rejoice [in it].
Or rather, what fruit could not be accomplished through association with the yogins of Śiva? (10)

Through association with great and virtuous persons—who understand the intent of the *Śivarahasya*, who rejoice in the bliss of Śiva, and who are the moving deities (*jaṅgamadeva*)—what fruit would not be accomplished?
The meaning is that everything will be accomplished. || 10 ||
Thus concludes the section on the greatness of the mobile [deities],
the section on the greatness of devotees,
and the introductory section; now follows the greatness of the devotee who is devoted to the greatness of the Guru, the Liṅga, and the mobile [deities].
He establishes this through twelve sūtras: [the first] verse [is so called] because it describes the greatness of the guru’s liṅga and of the Śiva-yogins.
The greatness of the devotee is already established; nevertheless, this is further praised. || 1 ||

The explanation is as follows: since devotion is practiced with a prior knowledge of such greatness toward the Guru, the Liṅga, and the Jangama, the greatness of the devotee is established; thus, he is praised in the scripture, meaning he is described with excellence. || 1 ||

Introduction: Now, regarding the question "Who are the devotees?"—in accordance with the meaning of the Śruti passage, "What one meditates upon with the mind, that one speaks with speech, and that one performs through action"—the author describes the nature of a devotee in this verse:
"Those who worship Mahādeva, the Supreme Self, the Imperishable..."
Those who [act] through deed, mind, or speech are proclaimed as devotees. || 2 ||

The meaning is that those who worship the Supreme Self, Mahādeva, in the form of the *liṅga*, through physical action consisting of adoration with both hands, through mental action consisting of meditation on the form of Śiva, and through vocal action consisting of praise, are called devotees (*bhakta*). 2.

Introduction: Regarding the question of whether there is a distinction of caste in devotion to Śiva, the verse says: "For devotion to Śiva, which carries one across the fear of saṃsāra, is indeed difficult to attain."
Wherever she resides, he is proclaimed as a true devotee.
The explanation is clear. || 3 ||

Introduction: Therefore, he says that for people who are tormented by birth and death, there is no need for any other virtuous deed apart from devotion to Śiva—verse: What is the use of the Vedas? What is the use of those scriptures? What is the use of sacrifices? What is the use of austerities and vows?
If there is no devotion to Śaṅkara for embodied beings who are diseased by birth, [then all is in vain]. (4)

The meaning is that the exposition is by means of treatises (*śāstra*) that follow the sense of the Vedas, such as the *Śiva-āgama*, the *Sūtras*, the *Purāṇas*, and so forth; the rest is clear. || 4 ||

Introduction: Now, [the author] states, by means of an illustration, that virtuous action performed apart from devotion to Śiva is fruitless and even yields contrary results: Verse: Even the meritorious deed of one devoid of devotion to Śiva is fruitless.
And even for a skillful performer at a great sacrifice, there may be a contrary result.
The explanation would be that the meaning is "it did not exist. || 5 ||

Introduction: Now, [the author] states, by means of an illustration, that even a wicked deed becomes a virtuous deed through devotion to Śiva: Verse: Even one who has committed extremely sinful deeds is purified through devotion to Śiva.
Just as in the past, through devotion, even Caṇḍa, though a slayer of his father, became Śiva.
The commentary: "Śiva" means the Lord of the hosts of Śivas; the rest is clear. || 6 ||

Introduction: Now, if this is so, one might ask whether or not there is a connection with merit and demerit for those devoted to Śiva; regarding this, the verse says: "Indeed, for a devotee of Śiva, there is neither good nor evil action."
For those devoid of devotion to Śiva, there is the binding of the fetters of karma.
The explanation is clear. || 7 ||
Introduction: To explain how this is so, he states it by means of two sūtras preceded by an illustration.
Verse: For living beings who have taken refuge in Śiva, there is no connection with karma.
How could there be fear born of darkness for the Lord of Day, who possesses swift steeds? || 8 ||

The meaning is that just as there is no fear caused by darkness for the horses of the Sun, the Lord of Day, so too there is no connection— that is, no association— with action consisting of merit and demerit for those devoted to Śiva. || 8 ||
Verse: It is not possible to obstruct the karma of those devoted to Śiva who are free from all fetters.
How could chains made of lotus fibers restrain intoxicated elephants?

Regarding the explanation: because the three impurities (*mala*), such as that of the individual soul (*āṇava*), have been removed through Śiva-initiation (*śivadīkṣā*), ritual action (*karman*) is neither capable nor able to restrain those whose devotion to Śiva is unimpeded. In this regard, there is an illustration: just as a chain made of lotus-fiber threads would not restrain an intoxicated elephant.
The meaning is "so it is. || 9 ||
Introduction: Therefore, he states that only a devotee of Śiva is worthy of worship:
"Whether he be a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or even a Śūdra..."
Or even an outcaste who is devoted to Śiva—he alone is to be honored like Śiva himself. || 10 ||
The explanation is clear. || 10 ||

Introduction: Now, one might object that since Śūdras and others are inferior in comparison to Brāhmaṇas and the like, how can they be equal to them? To this, he says in the verse: "When there is immersion in devotion to Śiva, what room is there for the conceptualization of caste?"
When the fuel has been consumed by fire, what distinction can possibly be proclaimed?
The explanation is clear. || 11 ||

Introduction: Having stated that "only those devoted to Śiva are the lords of the Gaṇas," he concludes the section on the greatness of devotion with this verse: "Pure, joined with observances, and having offered the fruits of their actions to Śiva..."
Those who worship Śiva in this world are to be known as the lords of the Gaṇas.

Those who are pure through exposition, purified by initiation (*dīkṣā*), perfected in their observances (*niyama*), observers of the *śiva-vrata*, whose acquisition of the fruits of action is offered to Śiva, and whose arrival at the fruits of merit and demerit is likewise offered to Him—those virtuous ones in the world worship the *śivaliṅga*. For one who is not Śiva himself, there is no worship of Śiva; Rudra cannot worship Rudra.
By such statements as these, the meaning is that they are to be known as the Gaṇeśvaras and the Rudras. || 12 ||

Thus ends the section on the majesty of devotion; now, the verse clarifies the nature of the Guru: "The syllable *gu* transcends the qualities (*guṇa*), and the syllable *ru* transcends form (*rūpa*)."
He who bestows that which transcends the qualities and is formless is known as a Guru.
The letter *gu* is the explanation; it is beyond the qualities of nature (*prakṛti-guṇa*). The letter *ru* is beyond the form of impure *māyā*, being beyond qualities and formless.
That which consists of the three mandalas, the three qualities, the luminous lunar digit (*bindu-kalā*), and the void consisting of consciousness—that is the Reality.
He who gives [instruction] and teaches is known as a guru; the meaning is that he is traditionally known as a "guru. || 8 ||

Introduction: Now, in this context, the author clarifies the nature of the teacher (ācārya) in a verse: "He gathers together the meanings of the scriptures and firmly establishes them in right conduct."
Because he practices it himself, he is therefore called an ācārya (teacher). || 9 ||

He explains by elucidating the meaning of the scriptures and the secret meanings of the Vīraśaiva scriptures; he establishes and disciplines his disciples thoroughly in the practice of Vīraśaiva conduct, and he himself practices that very Vīraśaiva conduct— for that reason, indeed, he is called an Ācārya.
The meaning is that, according to the *Kaṭhavallī* scripture—"One who has obtained this [teaching] is a skilled speaker"—the teacher is so designated. || 9 ||

Introduction: Having now provided the etymological definition of the word *deśika* (guide/teacher), he concludes the section on the *dīkṣāguru* (initiation teacher)—stated in two *sūtras* as being none other than the Guru of the World in the state of identity with the Śiva-liṅga—with the following verse: The verse: "That teacher who strives through the yoga that transcends the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*)..."
Śiva, the teacher of the universe, is the cause and the means for crossing the ocean of illusion. || 10 ||

"He who bestows liberation through the knowledge of the exposition is known as the *deśika*," according to the well-known statement of the *Kāmika*. This *deśika*, by means of the yoga that transcends the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvātīta-yoga*), [attains] the state beyond the path— the supreme goal of the path, O Lord of the Paths.
He who exerts himself—that is, remains diligent—through the yoga of transcending the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan) consisting of phonemes, words, and so forth, as established in the Śruti;
he is Śiva, unified with the Śivaliṅga, meaning he is the Teacher of the World who serves as the cause for the means of crossing the ocean of Māyā.
Introduction: Now, as to how he is the teacher of the world, the verse says: "By whom undivided consciousness is manifested in all things."
By the power of his own yoga, that Guru is the illuminator of the universe. || 11 ||

The explanation regarding all things: by the power of its own union with all things—namely, all objects such as blue, yellow, and so forth—consciousness (*caitanya*), which is indivisible and consists of existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānanda*), is manifested through the force of one's own experience;
for even at the time when specific objects such as blue or yellow appear, the indivisible consciousness persists as "I."

Therefore, it is made clear that otherwise there would be no perception of that which is to be known; thus, that Guru is the "illuminator of the universe," meaning the one who makes the universe manifest. || 11 ||
Thus concludes the section on the preceptor of initiation.
Now, the section on the Teacher of Training.
Introduction:

Now, according to the statement in the *Vātulottara*, "He by whom a disciple is taught through the means of knowledge in the relationship of the teacher and the taught is called a *śikṣāguru*," [the author] describes the section concerning the *śikṣāguru*.
This initiation-teacher is the cause of the disciple's training and the awakener of his understanding.
And one who expounds questions and answers is called a teacher of instruction (śikṣāguru). || 1 ||
The meaning is that this initiation guru, being the awakener of the disciple, is the expounder who provides answers to questions;
by giving the answer to a question posed by the disciple and acting as the cause of instruction—that is, the reason for teaching—he is called the "instruction guru. || 1 ||
Introduction: Now, he clarifies this very point with a verse: "This is clearly declared to be the awakener, and this is the object to be awakened."
He by whom the disciple is enjoined [in the training] is called the *śikṣāguru*. || 2 ||

The meaning of "explanation" (*vyākhyāna*) is that which reveals the doctrine of Śiva-siddhānta and illuminates the supreme reality (*paratattva*). This is because of the statement of the Grammarians: "There is no cognition in the world that occurs without the accompaniment of words. Thus, this knowledge of Śiva-yoga is clearly to be understood as having become manifest through the instruction of the Teacher (*deśika*), by means of which Guru [it is revealed].
The meaning is that one who is designated as a disciple (śiṣya) is instructed—that is, disciplined—and being thus guided, he is called a teacher of training (śikṣāguru). || 2 ||

Introduction: Now, the Teacher, following the Vedic tradition which states that "the Teacher is the prior form, the pupil is the subsequent form, and knowledge is the junction," describes its nature through these two aspects.
(Verse: These are like the rays of the autumnal moon, which dispel the darkness of saṃsāra.
He from whom words proceed is called an Ācārya.

They declare— that is, they speak of— that virtuous teacher whose words, which are the sentences of instruction, proceed like the rays of the autumnal moon for the destruction of the darkness of saṃsāra. || 3 ||
He who bestows the knowledge of the Lord, which turns back the illusion of the world.
They know that excellent teacher to be the means for the cultivation of the impression of non-duality.
He who provides— that is, reveals— the exposition which brings about the cessation of the world-illusion, the cessation of the delusion of duality regarding the phenomenal world,
and the knowledge of the Lord (pati), the Lord of the universe, the eternal, auspicious, and infallible Self— namely,
the knowledge of Śiva as non-different from one's own self as established in the Nārāyaṇopaniṣad; him [I salute].
They know him as the best of teachers, the most excellent of teachers; the meaning is that they recognize him as such. || 4 ||
Introduction: Now, with two sūtras, he states that the best of gurus is one who, being endowed with the knowledge of the non-duality of Śiva, is precisely the remover of the doubts of his disciples.
Verse: Having taken up the prima facie position consisting of the conceptualization of the difference between the world [and Śiva]...
This Guru, superior in virtues, has established the doctrine of non-duality (advaita). || 5 ||

Having taken up and accepted the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*)—which consists of an explanation involving the conceptualization of the world's diversity and is characterized by the twofold division of worldly distinctions—this teacher, who possesses the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) of non-duality (*advaita*), is indeed the teacher of instruction; the meaning is that he is superior and most excellent because of his excellence in virtues. || 5 ||
A battle-axe for the total eradication of the dense forest of doubt.
He whose stream of eloquent sayings is pure is the crest-jewel among teachers.

The commentary is pure and stainless; that stream of eloquent speech, which is the stream of the preceptor’s instructional words, is an axe for the total destruction of the thicket of the forest of doubt—a battle-axe for the complete clearing away of the wilderness of uncertainty.
He is the crest-jewel among preceptors; this is the meaning of "the most excellent. || 6 ||
Introduction: Now, he further elucidates the meaning by means of two sūtras.
[The first] verse: That which is always seen within the expanse of the stainless mirror of well-spoken words...
The glory of liberation, in the form of the lunar disc, is that Guru who delivers one across the ocean of existence. || 7 ||

In whose stainless mirror-disk of the words of instruction the Fortune of Liberation (mokṣalakṣmī) is seen—that is, shines forth—both as a direct form and as a reflected image, that Guru is the savior;
that is to say, he is the one who delivers [beings] from the ocean of saṃsāra. || 7 ||
Introduction: Now, he speaks by way of another method in a verse: "He who himself illuminates that which is to be inscribed upon the hearts of his disciples..."
Who could be equal to this Guru, who is the illuminator of knowledge?

Regarding the exposition: that glorious Guru who, by means of the lamp of knowledge—that is, the lamp of wisdom—illuminates and reveals the "painting on the heart," which is the image of his own nature situated within the lotus of the disciples' hearts;
who could be equal to this Guru? No one is equal to him.
This is the meaning. || 8 ||

Introduction: Regarding the question of whether such a guru exists, having stated that he is difficult to find, the section on the teacher of instruction is concluded with this verse: "By the bestowing of the supreme medicine of the realization of supreme non-duality..."
By whom is that Teacher, the destroyer of the disease of saṃsāra, obtained? || 9 ||
The meaning is that this explanation cannot be obtained by anyone who is devoid of Śiva’s compassion. || 9 ||
Thus ends the section on the Teacher of Training.
Now begins the section on the Guru of Knowledge.
Introduction: Now, that by which the knowledge contemplating the nature of Śiva is taught—

In accordance with the statement from the *Vātulottara*, "He who exists for the sake of attaining liberation for one desiring liberation is called the Guru of Knowledge," the section concerning the Guru of Knowledge is now described:
Verse: He is the one who causes the cutting away of doubts regarding the instructions of the teacher.
This one is known as the direct teacher of knowledge (jñānaguru), who bestows right knowledge. || 1 ||
The one who provides explanations of the instructions and their secret meanings, the instructor, the author of the teachings,
the one who cuts through doubt, the remover of the disciple's uncertainty— this very teacher of training is the one who correctly and directly bestows knowledge.
The meaning is that one who bestows the knowledge of Śiva that has become directly manifest is remembered as a "Guru of Knowledge" (jñānaguru). || 1 ||

Introduction: Now, as to the question of what the knowledge of Śiva (*śivajñāna*) is like and how it brings about direct perception (*pratyakṣīkaroti*), he says in this verse: "The sky of consciousness (*cidaṃbara*), free from modification and devoid of all differentiation of the universe."
He who realizes [the truth] through reasoning is called a knowledge-teacher (jñānaguru). || 2 ||

Through the power of the realization of emptiness— [expressed as] "I did not know anything," in which all worldly distinctions have been cast out— one seeks the subject of cognition, the sky of consciousness (*cidvyoma*), the space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*) free from modification, in which all diversity of the universe has been negated by means of reasoning, via the investigation of the cognizer of clearly manifest blue, pleasure, and so forth.

The meaning is this: since the attainment of the ultimate subject (pāramārthikapramātṛ) is taught here, he who makes it directly perceptible through the reasoning of his own experience as declared in the Śivādvaita scriptures is the "Guru of Knowledge" (jñānaguru). || 2 ||
Introduction: Now he introduces the knowledge of Śiva with two sūtras.
Verse: This moon possesses a stain and is subject to waxing and waning.
The moon of knowledge remains stainless and free from modification.

The explanation is as follows: while that moon is overwhelmed by and afflicted with waning and waxing, this moon of knowledge—the moon of consciousness—remains free from stain, meaning it remains changeless and devoid of transformation, existing without blemish. || 3 ||
A lamp fashioned from jewels destroys the darkness situated at its side.
The lamp of awakening, which is unrestrained, destroys all-pervading darkness.

The meaning is that just as a lamp made of jewels or gems dispels the darkness situated nearby, so too does the lamp of awakening—the lamp of consciousness—unrestrained and unimpeded, dispel the darkness existing everywhere; it is all-pervading and removes the darkness present in all places. || 4 ||
Introduction: Now, with two aphorisms, he introduces the venerable Guru, who is intent upon the instruction of the knowledge of Śiva.
Verse: He is devoted to the teaching of the specific knowledge that accomplishes all goals.
Śiva is the teacher of knowledge, the benefactor of all. || 5 ||

The Knowledge-Guru alone— who is devoted to the teaching of the specific Śiva-knowledge that accomplishes all purposes characterized by both worldly enjoyment and liberation— is the direct Śiva who bestows grace upon all those seeking liberation.
This is the meaning. || 5 ||
The verse: His sidelong glance is a moon that increases the ocean of wisdom.
That guru, who has reached the further shore of knowledge, is the cutter of the darkness of saṃsāra.

The commentary: That teacher whose moon-like glance increases the ocean of the knowledge of Śiva and cuts through the darkness of saṃsāra—he is the Guru, the Illustrious Guru (Śrī-guru), who has reached the further shore of knowledge; the meaning is that he has attained the ultimate limit of both supreme and non-supreme knowledge. || 6 ||
Introduction: Now, describing that very Guru as the Sun, he establishes his superiority even over him with this verse: "This Sun is proclaimed to be the dispeller of external darkness."
The all-pervading Sun of Teachers, who cuts through the darkness both within and without. || 7 ||
This exposition is the sun; it cuts through external darkness, it is the dispeller of outer gloom.

It is the all-pervasive Lord, the sun that illumines consciousness, the teacher-sun who severs both outer and inner darkness. "I am not Śiva"—this is the ignorance residing in the objects of the senses. [I am] not Śiva.
Thus, he is proclaimed as one who pierces the internal knowledge.
Introduction: Having thus indicated the knowledge of Śiva (*śivajñāna*), which makes Śiva known, [the author] concludes the section on the Guru of Knowledge (*jñānaguru*) with two aphorisms.
Verse: Without even a mere fraction of a sidelong glance, and without the conceptualization of meditation and so forth...
Wherever one contemplates the state of Śiva-ness, that is considered the Śāmbhava Veda.

Without the conceptualization of explanations, meditations, dhāraṇās, and so forth, one should contemplate Śivatva through the mere glance of the compassionate side-long look of the venerable Guru; that which becomes manifest is considered—and this is the accepted view—to be the Śāmbhava Veda. || 8 ||
The verse: By whom this most pure knowledge, which places one in the hand of Śiva, has been bestowed;
The disciple shall become liberated while living, and the guru shall be an ocean of knowledge.

Regarding the commentary: when the illustrious Guru—who is skilled in making manifest the Śiva-nature of one's own self—bestows the stainless knowledge of Śiva upon the hand of the seeker of Śiva (the disciple), that disciple becomes liberated even while living; such a Guru is the "Ocean of the Knowledge of Śiva"—this is the meaning. || 9 ||

And as soon as it was obtained, the remainder in the house [was used] for his own livelihood.
He who worships the mobile [deities] with devotion has indeed worshipped me alone. || 88 ||
O Īśānī, my very form is present in person through [the offerings of] bedding, seating, and food.
One who is helpless, diseased, miserable, mute, or even deaf; || 89 ||
One should not despise a person who bears the sectarian marks (liṅgin), even if he is lame, shaven-headed, or of bad conduct.
O Goddess, no quarrel should be waged among one another by those who are yogis of Śiva.
Neither slander, nor envy, nor malice, nor even oppression.

He who worships the moving [deity], the Lord who is my very own form in person.
He has indeed honored me; therefore, O Goddess, I am he—of this there is no doubt. || 11 ||
Therefore, one who possesses devotion and is capable [should act] toward those great-souled ones who are still subject to transmigration.
Know that, O Śivā, it is indeed a place of devotion and is exceedingly dear to me.
He who is always devoted to the worship of the Liṅga according to the path taught by his guru.
One should worship mobile beings according to one's ability; for he is remembered as a true devotee of Maheśvara.
One who possesses devotion among my devotees should worship the liṅga three times a day.
O Dear One, he who is devoted to the practice of his own doctrine is indeed a Māheśvara.
O Goddess, this reality of water is another body of mine.
And I am his presiding deity; O Goddess, I am he, without a doubt. || 15 ||
But he who possesses the characteristics already described is fit for conduct and for the worship of the mobile [deity].
Know, O Śivā, that this place is Māheśvara, which is exceedingly dear to me.
O Maheśānī, he who does not worship the unoffered [liṅga], even without worshipping the jaṅgamas (the moving forms).
One should neither eat nor abandon what has been offered to me, even if one is in a state of great distress.
This very one is said to be grace; he is none other than myself, without a doubt.
Know that place of His grace, O Śivā, to be exceedingly dear to me.
